displayQuote: Let's win one for the Gipper

meta.title: Who really said "Let's win one for the Gipper"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Rockne said it, but he was quoting a dead player. The words are George Gipp’s, and Rockne first published them in 1930 — two years after the game.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Let's win one for the Gipper'?
meta.ogDescription: Rockne’s most famous line was not his. He was quoting George Gipp’s deathbed request — and he only published it two years after the game.

answer.label: Not Knute Rockne — actually George Gipp
answer.authorDates: 1895–1920 · Notre Dame halfback — the school’s first Walter Camp All-American
answer.sourceLine: Rockne delivered the line, but he wrote it down as someone else’s. In his own telling — published in Collier’s and carried by the Associated Press in December 1930 ↗ — the words belong to George Gipp, dying in a South Bend hospital in 1920: “tell them to go in there with all they have got and win just one for the Gipper.” Rockne says only that at half-time against Army in 1928 he “told the boys what he had said.” He never records his own words, and the imperative form everybody quotes — “Let’s win one for the Gipper” — appears in no source we could find from the period.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: George Gipp’s, as reported by Knute Rockne
Late 1920, as Gipp was dying; he died 14 December 1920
In Collier’s; reprinted by the Associated Press, Daily Alaska Empire, 16 December 1930, p. 5
Notre Dame 12, Army 6 — Yankee Stadium, 10 November 1928
Not documented in any period source we located

source.excerpt: “I’ve got to go, Rock,” he said. “It’s all right. I’m not afraid.” His eyes brightened. “Some time, Rock, when the team’s up against it, when things are wrong and the breaks are beating the boys — tell them to go in there with all they have got and win just one for the Gipper. I don’t know where I’ll be then, Rock, but I’ll know about it and I’ll be happy.”
trail: We read the earliest printing we could find of Rockne’s own version: an Associated Press column by sports editor Alan Gould in the Daily Alaska Empire (Juneau), 16 December 1930, page 5 ↗, introduced as “one of the greatest in football as Knute Rockne retold it in Colliers”. It prints Gipp’s request in the first person and then Rockne’s half-time account: “For the first time since Gipp’s death I told the boys what he had said.” It does not quote Rockne’s own words to the team.

We then checked Rockne against Rockne. His signed report of that very game, filed the day it was played and printed in the South Bend News-Times of 11 November 1928, page 29 ↗ under the headline “Knute Rockne Explains Irish Grid Triumph”, opens: “The effect of psychology on football teams was never more clearly demonstrated than it was here in the Yankee stadium Saturday afternoon.” It runs to about a thousand words on defensive schemes and substitutions. George Gipp is not mentioned anywhere on that page.

The game itself is solid. The same South Bend News-Times page ↗ carries the banner “NOTRE DAME STUNS ARMY AND CHRIS CAGLE BY 12-6” and Westbrook Pegler’s report datelined New York, 10 November, with Jack Chevigny scoring the tying touchdown and John O’Brien catching the winner.

Wikiquote ↗ hedges the line the same way we do: it lists “Let’s win one for the Gipper” only as a half-time statement “as portrayed in Knute Rockne, All American (1940)”, and files the full speech text under the 1940 screenplay by Robert Buckner rather than under Rockne. Wikipedia ↗ likewise says Gipp “was alleged to have said” the words.

author.name: George Gipp
author.kicker: The man whose words they were
author.heading: About George Gipp
author.metaLine: 1895–1920 · Notre Dame halfback · the school’s first Walter Camp All-American
author.bio: George Gipp (18 February 1895 – 14 December 1920) came to Notre Dame meaning to play baseball and was recruited onto the football team by Knute Rockne with no organised experience in the sport. He played halfback, quarterback and punter, became the school’s first Walter Camp All-American, and died at twenty-five, weeks after his last game, of pneumonia and a related infection. Everything anyone knows about his last words comes from Rockne, who published them ten years later.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Almost everything about this quotation gets shifted one step from where the evidence puts it: the speaker, the wording, and the year.

items.why: Rockne said something at half-time in 1928 and he is the reason the words survive — but in his own published account the sentence is George Gipp’s, and Rockne writes only that he “told the boys what he had said”. He never sets down his own phrasing. See the 1930 reprint ↗.

The documented sentence is Gipp’s — “win just one for the Gipper” — and even Wikiquote’s text of the 1940 screenplay ↗ keeps the “just”. The imperative “Let’s…” form is a later compression; we found it in no period source.

The Warner Bros. film, with Pat O’Brien as Rockne and Ronald Reagan as Gipp, is why the phrase is common currency. Wikiquote ↗ attributes the speech as filmed to the screenwriter Robert Buckner, not to Rockne.

Reagan, who played Gipp in the film, carried the phrase into politics: Wikipedia ↗ records him telling Vice President Bush at the 1988 Republican National Convention, “George, go out there and win one for the Gipper.”

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is George Gipp’s, as Knute Rockne reported it a decade after Gipp’s death; the famous wording is the public’s. Rockne’s own 1930 telling ↗ is the document to read.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Notre Dame beat Army 12–6 at Yankee Stadium on 10 November 1928, after a season Rockne later described as punishing — beaten by Wisconsin, beaten by Georgia Tech, “all but demoralized”. The result is in the next morning’s papers. The half-time speech about George Gipp is not: it surfaces two years later, in a story Rockne told in Collier’s, and the distance between those two dates is the whole question about this quotation.

It is not a small gap. Rockne wrote his own game analysis that weekend, attributed the win to “the effect of psychology”, spent about a thousand words on it, and never named George Gipp. Then, in 1930, he supplied the psychology’s content.
detailsBody: None of this proves the half-time speech never happened. Rockne is a witness, he was there, and no contemporary account contradicts him; he simply did not mention it at the time. What it does mean is that the only chain of custody for Gipp’s words runs through one man, telling the story ten years after the death and two years after the game, in a national magazine, about the most famous football programme in the country. Wikipedia’s phrasing is the honest one: Gipp “was alleged to have said” it.

The detail that survives best is not Rockne’s at all. In the same 1930 account Rockne reports that as Jack Chevigny scored, he shouted “That’s one for the Gipper!” Chevigny’s touchdown is right there in the 11 November 1928 game reports, tying the score in the third quarter. The line and the moment are attested; who said what in the locker room is not.
context.pull: The game is in the next morning’s papers. The speech arrives two years later.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Daily Alaska Empire of 16 December 1930, page 5, carries an Associated Press column by Alan Gould introducing a story 'as Knute Rockne retold it in Colliers', printing Gipp's words 'tell them to go in there with all they have got and win just one for the Gipper', and Rockne's statement that at half-time against Army in 1928 'For the first time since Gipp's death I told the boys what he had said.'
The same 1930 column reports that as Chevigny scored the winning touchdown he said 'That's one for the Gipper!'

The South Bend News-Times of 11 November 1928, page 29, is headlined 'NOTRE DAME STUNS ARMY AND CHRIS CAGLE BY 12-6', carries Westbrook Pegler's report datelined New York, Nov. 10, and carries Knute Rockne's own signed column 'Knute Rockne Explains Irish Grid Triumph' datelined Yankee Stadium, New York, Nov. 10, which begins with 'The effect of psychology on football teams' and does not mention George Gipp anywhere on the page.

Wikiquote lists 'Let's win one for the Gipper' only as a half-time statement 'as portrayed in Knute Rockne, All American (1940)', and files the full speech text under the 1940 screenplay by Robert Buckner, whose text reads 'win just one for the Gipper'.

George Gipp lived 18 February 1895 to 14 December 1920, was Notre Dame's first Walter Camp All-American, was recruited by Rockne despite no organised football experience, 'was alleged to have said' the deathbed line, was portrayed by Ronald Reagan in the 1940 film, and Reagan told Vice President Bush at the 1988 Republican National Convention 'George, go out there and win one for the Gipper.'
